items.name: USB power bank for phones
items.need: A charged power bank keeps a phone working for calls, alerts and maps for several days when the wall outlets are dead.
items.how_to_choose: For a phone, 10,000 mAh gives roughly two full charges and fits in a pocket; 20,000 to 27,000 mAh gives four or more and weighs about a pound or more. A bank under 100 Wh can go in airline carry-on, which is where most power banks stop; a larger one needs the airline's approval. Look for USB-C Power Delivery of 20 W or more. Before buying any power bank, check the exact model number against CPSC recalls: millions of units from well-known brands were recalled in 2024 to 2026. Avoid no-name banks sold only through marketplaces, which make up most of the recent recalls.

qty.note: One for each adult and teenager aged 14 or over who carries a phone. Add one for a younger child who carries a phone.

items.already_own: A power bank you already own is fine if it is not on a recall list, is not swollen, cracked or hot when charging, and still charges your phone at least once. Look up the model number printed on the case at cpsc.gov/Recalls and on the maker's recall page. Recharge it every three months.

safety_notes.text: Buy batteries and battery products that are listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory. Use the charging equipment supplied with or made for the device, and stop charging once the battery is full.

Stop using a lithium-ion battery if you notice an odor, a change in color or shape, too much heat, leaking or odd noises. Store spare batteries at room temperature, away from anything that can burn. Do not put them in the trash; take an ordinary used one to a battery recycling location. A damaged or recalled one is handled differently: see the next two notes.
Do not store batteries where they would block the only way out of a room.

On aircraft, power banks count as spare lithium batteries: carry-on only, never in checked bags. Up to 100 Wh needs no approval. From 101 to 160 Wh you need airline approval and may carry two at most. Airlines may set stricter limits.

A recalled lithium power bank does not go in the trash, in curbside recycling or in a store's battery box, because it is a greater fire risk than an ordinary used battery. Follow the recall notice, and ask your local household hazardous-waste center whether it takes recalled lithium batteries before you carry one there. Treat a damaged power bank (swollen, cracked, leaking or hot) the same way.

safety_notes.text: If a lithium-ion battery is damaged, ask the maker of the battery or the device how to handle it. Lithium-ion batteries, and devices that contain them, do not go in household trash or recycling bins.

items.name: Compact portable power station (200 to 350 Wh)
items.need: A small battery with a household outlet keeps phones, a light, a Wi-Fi router or a small fan running through an evening, with no fumes and no noise. It is too small to run a 40-watt medical device for a full night.
items.how_to_choose: Check two numbers, not one. Capacity in watt-hours (Wh) sets how long it runs: add up watts times hours for what you will plug in and compare that with about 85% of the printed Wh. Output in watts sets what it can run at all: everything switched on at the same moment must stay under the continuous AC watts. Where you can, measure real use with a plug-in watt meter or the station's own display instead of trusting a label, because a charger's printed watts are its maximum, not what the device uses. Choose lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4 or LFP) cells, which last thousands of cycles, and check the weight, since you may carry it up stairs. A UPS or pass-through mode lets it sit between the wall and a router and take over when power drops. Compare prices with the 1,000 Wh class before you buy.

qty.note: Optional extra: no baseline quantity. Buy one only if your power audit calls for it.

items.already_own: Any portable power station you own will do if it holds a charge, has not been recalled, and passes both checks: 85% of its printed Wh covers the watts times hours you need, and its continuous output is above the total watts you will run at once. Time it once with the real devices before you depend on it.

safety_notes.text: Never use a fuel-burning generator inside a home or garage, even with doors and windows open. Use one outside only, at least 20 feet from the home with the exhaust pointing away. An apartment balcony cannot meet that distance, so a battery power station is the option for apartments.

Generators and fuel should always be used outdoors and at least 20 feet away from windows, doors and attached garages. Install carbon monoxide detectors with battery backup on every level of the home.

Buy battery products listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory. Use the charging equipment made for the device. Stop using it if the battery shows an unusual odor, excessive heat, popping sounds, swelling or a change in color. Do not store batteries where they block the only exit from a room.
Do not charge lithium-ion batteries below 32 F or above 105 F. Store them at room temperature, away from anything that can burn.

If you use a medical device that needs electricity, tell your electric company and fire department, and ask the device maker or supplier whether it can run on batteries. When power returns, check that the device settings have not changed.
safety_notes.source_title: FDA Offers Tips about Medical Devices and Natural Disasters

safety_notes.text: Know how long any battery that supports your equipment will last, test backup power regularly, and plan for an outage of several days even if your utility has you on a priority reconnection list.
safety_notes.source_title: Emergency Power Planning for People Who Use Electricity and Battery-Dependent Assistive Technology and Medical Devices

safety_notes.text: Talk to your medical provider about a power outage plan for any medical device that runs on electricity.

When you store a power station, turn off all of its outputs, keep it somewhere cool and dry, and charge it fully at least once every three months. Follow your own station's manual where it says something different.

item_flags: Power for a medical device is life-safety. The device's maker and the user's clinician decide what backup is safe, not this site. Nothing on this page is a recommendation to run a CPAP, an oxygen concentrator or any other medical device from these stations.

Do the arithmetic before you rely on one: a 40-watt device for 8 hours needs 320 Wh before losses, which is more than any station in this 200 to 350 Wh class holds. The 40-watt figures in the picks are arithmetic from an example, not tests: a real CPAP or other device, its settings and its humidifier change the answer, so measure your own.

Power stations recalled from 2024 to 2026 include the EcoFlow Delta Max 2000 (model EFD310), the Goal Zero Yeti 3000X, the Harbor Freight Predator 2000W, the HALO 1000 and Klein Tools and Blackfire models, and CPSC warned against Aeiusny 400W and 500W stations: check any station you own at cpsc.gov/Recalls.

items.name: Large portable power station (1,000 Wh and up)
items.need: A large battery station can keep a refrigerator cold for a day or more and run lights, phones and a router for days, all indoors and without fuel.
items.how_to_choose: Start from the load, and check two numbers. Capacity in watt-hours (Wh) sets how long it runs: a refrigerator that averages about 50 W over a day would get about 17 hours from 1,000 Wh and about a day and a half from 2,000 Wh. Output in watts sets what it can run at all: everything switched on at once, and the surge when a refrigerator's motor starts, must stay under the station's limits. Where you can, measure your own appliance over a full day with a plug-in watt meter instead of multiplying the label by 24, because a refrigerator cycles on and off. Choose LiFePO4 cells and a UPS mode. Weight rises with capacity: about 25 lb for 1,000 Wh, 36 to 40 lb for 2,000 Wh and about 74 lb for 3,000 Wh. Home-backup stations of about 4,000 Wh with 240 V output weigh 110 to 140 lb; they roll on wheels and take two people on stairs. Without a way to recharge, any battery is a one-time supply, so plan where you would recharge it: a building with a generator, a workplace, a car or a solar panel. Of these picks, only EcoFlow's page says its station is certified to UL 2743 standards; the Anker and Jackery pages state no listing, and no station of their size with a listing stated on its maker's page was found, so check for a UL or ETL mark on the unit.

qty.note: Optional extra: no baseline quantity. Buy one only if your power audit calls for it.

items.already_own: A power station you already own is good enough if 85% of its rated watt-hours covers your critical load for the hours you need, its continuous output is above the total watts you will run at once, and it has not been recalled. Test it once with the real appliance, timing how long it lasts, before you depend on it.

safety_notes.text: Never use a generator inside your home or garage, even if doors and windows are open. Run generators outdoors, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents. A balcony cannot meet that distance.

Never use portable generators inside homes or garages. Use them outside only, at least 20 feet from the home with the exhaust facing away. Install battery-operated carbon monoxide alarms, or alarms with battery backup, on every level and outside sleeping areas.

With no thermometer, treat fridge food as unsafe once the power has been off for 4 hours with the door kept shut. With a thermometer in the fridge, throw out meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers once they have been above 40 °F for more than 2 hours. Frozen food that still has ice crystals, or is at 40 °F or colder, can be refrozen or cooked. Never taste food to test it.

safety_notes.text: Throw out food that has been at 40 °F or higher for two hours or more. If the power is out for more than a day, discard medicine that should be refrigerated unless the label says otherwise.

If you rely on home medical equipment that needs electricity, ask your doctor or provider how to keep it running in an outage, ask your power provider to put you on a list for priority restoration, and keep a cooler and ice packs for medicines that must stay cold.

Tell your electric company and fire department that you have a medical device that needs power. Ask the maker or supplier whether the device can run on batteries, and check its settings when power returns.
safety_notes.source_title: FDA Offers Tips about Medical Devices and Natural Disasters

safety_notes.text: Know the working time of any battery that supports your equipment, check backup power regularly, and plan for a multi-day outage even if you are on a priority reconnection list.

safety_notes.text: Buy battery products listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory, use the charger made for them, and stop using them if you notice odor, excessive heat, popping sounds, swelling or a change in color. Do not store them where they block the only exit from a room.

When you store a power station, turn off all of its outputs, keep it somewhere cool and dry, and charge it fully at least once every three months. Follow your own station's manual where it says something different.

items.name: Portable solar panel
items.need: A solar panel is the only way to refill a power station during a long outage if you have no car and nowhere else to plug in.
items.how_to_choose: A plug that fits is not a panel that is compatible. Check the panel against your station's input limits before you buy: its open-circuit voltage must be below the station's maximum input volts, with room to spare because voltage rises in the cold, and its current and watts must be within what the station's maker allows. If the station's maker does not name the pairing, ask the maker before you buy an adapter cable. Wherever it will sit, a panel needs direct sun on its face, and real output is below the rating even outdoors (the best 200 W panels measured 170 to 185 W in full sun). Folding panels of 100 to 200 W weigh about 4 to 19 lb. Folding 400 W panels refill a large station about twice as fast and weigh 30 to 38 lb. A rigid glass panel costs less per watt, but it weighs about 25 lb, does not fold and has to be mounted or propped securely. Check the size and weight against where you will store it and set it up, and never hang or prop a panel where it could fall from a balcony or window.

qty.note: Optional extra: no baseline quantity. Buy one only if you own a power station and have a yard, a balcony, roof access or a window that gets direct sun.

items.already_own: A panel you already own works if its open-circuit voltage is below your station's maximum solar input voltage, its current and watts are within the station's limits, and its plug fits or the station's maker sells the adapter. Test it on a sunny day and note how many watts the station shows.

safety_notes.text: Use charging equipment that is made for the device, and buy products listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory. Stop using a battery that shows odor, excessive heat, popping sounds, swelling or a change in color.

Do not charge lithium-ion batteries below 32 F or above 105 F. A power station left in direct summer sun beside its panel can exceed that, so keep the station in the shade or indoors and run only the cable to the panel.

item_flags: Output behind window glass and on shaded or north-facing balconies is far below the rating: treat window charging as a slow trickle and test your own spot before relying on it.

items.name: Charging from a car (USB-C car charger or plug-in inverter)
items.need: For households with a car, the vehicle's 12 V socket can recharge phones, power banks and a small power station during a long outage.
items.how_to_choose: A USB-C Power Delivery car charger is enough for phones, tablets and power banks. A plug-in inverter adds a household outlet, but a 12 V socket is limited by its fuse: roughly 120 W on a 10 A socket and 150 to 180 W on a 15 A socket, so an inverter rated above that gains nothing from the socket. Charging with the engine off drains the starting battery; do not run small loads for more than about an hour without starting the car, and only ever run the engine outdoors. Many power stations also sell their own 12 V car charging cable, which is often the simplest route.

qty.note: One per household that has a car. Skip this item if you have no vehicle.

items.already_own: A car charger or inverter you already own is fine if it charges your phone at a normal speed and does not get hot. For an inverter, check that its plug matches your socket's fuse rating in the owner's manual.

safety_notes.text: Never run your car or truck inside a garage that is attached to a house, even with the garage door open. Carbon monoxide from the exhaust can kill without warning.
Install battery-operated carbon monoxide alarms, or alarms with battery backup, on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas.
Use only charging equipment made for the device, and stop using a battery that shows odor, excessive heat, popping sounds, swelling or a change in color.

items.name: Wall charger and cables
items.need: A fast multi-port charger and the right cables let you fill every phone, power bank and light before a storm, and recharge them from a power station afterward.
items.how_to_choose: Choose a GaN USB-C Power Delivery charger with enough ports to charge everything at once: 30 W covers one phone, 65 W or more covers a phone, a power bank and a tablet together. Keep one cable per device plus a spare: USB-C to USB-C rated 60 W or more, and an Apple MFi-certified USB-C to Lightning cable for an iPhone 14 or older. Braided nylon or silicone cables last longer than thin stock ones. Charging phones from a power station's USB-C port wastes less energy than using its AC outlet with a wall charger.

qty.note: One charger per household, plus one cable for each device and one spare.

items.already_own: The chargers and cables that came with your phones are good enough if you have one for every device and none is frayed, bent or hot in use. Check that you own a cable for each connector type in the home: USB-C, Lightning and any micro-USB devices such as older flashlights.

safety_notes.text: Use charging equipment that is supplied with or made for your device, buy products listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory, and stop charging once the battery is full.
Stop using a lithium-ion battery if you notice an odor, a change in color or shape, too much heat, leaking or odd noises. Choose certified products.

For large lithium batteries such as e-bike packs, CPSC says to be present while charging and never to charge while asleep or away from home. The same habit is sensible when charging a power station or several power banks at once before a storm.
